items.question: How do you see the role of GPUs in an AI inference market with different application needs?
items.object: GPUs and specialization in the AI inference market
items.answer: Something we've been saying for a long time: depending on where you are doing the influencing, what your target markets are, what applications you're going after, you can't really build a single chip that serves all of influencing's needs, right? And so, you've got to really break it down. And not every company is playing in every pocket of the market. You can't, right? Now, GPUs, just because they are so general, the ecosystem is so broad, clearly GPUs can go into many different applications for inference. But they're not going to be very efficient because of that. They're very broad in their applicability, they're general purpose, but when it comes to certain breakaway applications, where application need a very specific metric fully optimized, then GPUs will not do well in that market. I think the way to look at it is, you have the influencing market, it's going to be the largest part of AI compute. It's expected to be over a trillion-dollar market, call it in the next 5 years. GPUs will play in that market, clearly, but there's going to be portions or segments of that trillion dollars that will need lots of optimization, a highly optimized silicon.

items.question: Why do you think users are willing to pay a premium for low-latency AI inference?
items.object: Interactivity and the premium token economy
items.answer: The one that is truly breaking out right now is the segment that is called low-latency compute. Low-latency inference is specifically around applications that need high levels of interactivity. A great example would be cloud code. This happened months ago and you have people who are not programmers who are now using cloud code and are great programmers, right? The joke is, the new programming language is English. Everyone can program and you can be an ace programmer and you know how to prompt the model and how to use it. But that has led to people wanting to interact, and the faster the model is when it responds back to the user, the more likely the user is to stay with the threads, with the application. So, I think interactivity has become very important and companies are beginning to charge more for those high levels of interactivity. You can always say, "Look, I don't want that level of interactivity." In which case, I'll pay, call it $2 for a million tokens. But if I want that high level of interactivity, I'll pay $20 for a million tokens and people are willing to pay that $20. They want that interactivity. So, I think given that this new tier of inferencing is emerging, this new tier of tokens is emerging, we call it a premium token economy. We'll look at the entire token economy, which is inference. This is the premium token economy.

items.question: How do you understand d-Matrix's architectural advantage in the emerging premium token economy?
items.object: Compute architecture and d-Matrix's opportunity in low-latency inference
items.answer: Not many companies play in that segment because you need a specific compute architecture that is well suited for that fast token generation, right? So, it's about generating tokens very quickly and that typically means you have an architecture that puts compute and memory together in a way where you have order of magnitude more memory bandwidth available to your compute than a GPU would have. Because GPUs are based on HBM and they have a certain cap on the amount of memory bandwidth. Solutions like D Matrix, and you mentioned Groq and Cerebras, are the other architectures that allow compute to get access to very fast memory. And it's an order of magnitude faster than HBM. So, that is the breakaway category right now and D-Matrix falls into that breakaway category. And because that category has exploded on us literally in the last few months, we're just trying to keep up and I think we need to scale up into that opportunity rapidly.

items.question: How do you see the rise of agentic tools such as OpenClaw changing the importance of latency?
items.object: Agentic tools and latency-sensitive machine-to-machine communication
items.answer: I mean, OpenClaw. I mean, what happened with OpenClaw at the end of last year? We haven't even seen the full fallout of that, but you've seen a lot of agentic tools now being unleashed, right? Claude is incorporating a lot of agentic capabilities, right? Pretty much every enterprise-class software tool is trying to incorporate agentic capabilities. But I think to me, two things, right? One is Claude Code and the significant improvement in capabilities there, and then OpenClaw. So, this is agentic communication, machine-to-machine communication, where machines are, you know, you can spawn multiple agents across multiple virtual machines and a task is broken down into multiple agents. These agents are talking to each other, essentially orchestrating all the different work or the workflows that you have running on your computer. And now that is very latency-sensitive communication because machines are just waiting for other machines to finish tasks, right? And you don't want that to happen for too long, so latency begins to matter.

items.question: How do you think about expanding d-Matrix’s chiplet platform into edge computing?
items.object: Expanding d-Matrix’s chiplet platform into edge computing
items.answer: We could. Absolutely we could. We are not currently. The platform, the way we have built it, is a platform that is built with a LEGO block approach, right? We have these chiplets that are the LEGO block and then we can scale the solution up. We can put many chiplets together into a very large solution. So, for the cloud market and the data center market, we essentially take our chiplet approach and we package close to eight of them on a single card and we have 64 cards in a rack. So, we call it rack scale. We have 64 cards, each with eight chiplets, right? So, that gives you an idea of how many chiplets we sprinkle through the rack, right? But you don't have to. If you went into an edge market application where you're just doing, say, for example, if it's a robot, a physical AI application, or autonomous driving, right, where you need AI capabilities, you don't need that many chips. You might need a few chips and we can actually do that because of the LEGO block approach. We just scale it down, sprinkle fewer LEGO blocks into a physical AI application or an autonomous application. And the software would not change. The software is essentially built to scale with more chiplets or less chiplets, right? So, the platform is being built today to go into the edge market. However, the edge market is very fragmented. So, everyone has a slightly different software stack and each vertical—like, say, if you go to the physical AI vertical, the software stack looks different. Autonomous vertical, software stack looks different. Or industrial, the software stack looks different. So, we just don't have the scale today as a company to go address all these markets while we are trying to address the data center market. So, our goal is to stay focused on the data center market, then at the right time when the company has scale, we will branch out into other markets.

items.question: How closely has the emergence of interactive inference and agentic AI matched your original vision for d-Matrix?
items.object: The rapid emergence of interactive inference and agentic AI
items.answer: Now, I wish I could sit here and say I saw it all, I envisioned it all. No, I think that some of it we did, some of it was luck, obviously, and the luck is really about how quickly a lot of this stuff happened and how useful a lot of this stuff became so quickly. So, I think that that certainly caught even us by surprise, how quickly this is maturing. And this is because AI is learning fast, and AI is actually learning to help itself. There's this iterative recursive loop where as AI gets smart, it learns to build tools that it can use in more efficient ways and more capable ways. So, I think you have this very quick positive feedback loop that is the virtuous cycle that is underway, and that's why you're seeing the impact is just so rapid. But we had a broad idea. We said, okay, the bet was on inference first, right when we started the company, and then we said inference is going to be the big application, but then it's not just going to be about inference, it's going to be about interactive inference, and then it's not just about interactive inference, but it's about spawning machines that can take all of that interaction and do something with it. So, I think we kind of had a broader vision of how this could evolve, but it's even surprised us and pleasantly surprised us at how it's all come together so quickly.

items.question: What excites you about the prospect of AI agents developing organizational capabilities?
items.object: Teams of AI agents and organizational capabilities
items.answer: I think what we would be most excited by next is, I think we have seen agentic capabilities unleashed. I think we haven't yet truly seen organizational capabilities unleashed. So, meaning you have humans spawning agents and augmenting humans, but can you create teams of agents? And so, the abstraction of the task will keep going higher and higher. Right now, the tasks that are getting abstracted are like, okay, I want to extract this data from this database, prepare a PowerPoint presentation based on the data for a board meeting that I have in a few hours, call it. And the agents can go spawn up and do a task like that. Now imagine we start abstracting to a higher and higher level. When you say, wait, it's not just about mundane tasks that I want to get done on a day-to-day basis. Imagine if you could just describe a task at an extremely high level. Like, look, I have a customer that I want to win, and you go figure out who the decision makers are, what my product needs to be changed to. And so this thing comes with a whole strategy, like what an entire sales team and a marketing team would essentially do collectively, these agents could go spawn off and create a whole strategy plan. So, I think the tasks will get more and more abstracted as you go higher. And very soon, I think people talk about organizations being entirely run by agents. And then, where are we and how far are we from that? items.question: Why do you prefer Claude’s enterprise tools over OpenClaw for deploying AI agents across your organization?

items.answer: So, OpenClaw, I mean, we don't use OpenClaw because it's an open source framework. So there's obviously security concerns around what the agents are doing behind the scenes. We don't know yet, right? There is a certain level of transparency that's missing, but we use Claude Cowork. So, now Anthropic is incorporating all the same agentic capabilities that OpenClaw has into Claude Cowork. So, we have Claude Cowork Enterprise, Claude Code Enterprise, right? We have this agentic layer that comes along with the Claude tools that are available to the whole organization. So, yes, they can unleash agents across multiple different applications. items.question: Why do you think the cloud will remain attractive to startups building AI applications?
items.object: Cloud adoption by startups
items.answer: I think a lot of the outflow that happened to the cloud was smaller companies, companies looking to get started. I'll talk about D-Matrix. When we got started, we didn't want to deal with an on-prem cloud, right? We could just offload our entire IT infrastructure to somebody like an AWS or a Microsoft Azure and you were up and running in days, as opposed to setting up our own data center, setting up our own hardware. Even if it's in a colo, doing all of that was the traditional model even for small companies once upon a time, where you set up your own small data center, and you ran your own hardware, right? And we didn't have to do any of that. Didn't have to worry about security. Didn't have to worry about scaling that hardware, deploying the tools. None of that, right? So, that trend has been very strong and will stay strong even to this day. All the AI native startups, companies that are building these new age applications for AI, they're all running in the cloud. They're all still running in the cloud, right?

items.question: How do you interpret the apparent shift from cloud services back to private data centers as large enterprises adopt AI?
items.object: AI adoption in large enterprises with hybrid cloud infrastructure
items.answer: I think what you're talking about is maybe companies that were further along in their journey, much larger mid-size to large-size software companies, Fortune 500 companies that carry a lot of data. See, they never fully migrated to the cloud, right? There were applications that they migrated to the cloud, but there were certain applications that they didn't migrate into the cloud. There were certain things that were data sensitive. Their data never migrated into the cloud. Now, the only thing that is different now is you still have the same structure. It's a hybrid approach for some of these larger organizations where some of their applications run in the cloud, but some of their applications that tap into their native or domain-specific data, they don't want to have those applications running in the cloud. So, they're maintaining both. They're maintaining an on-prem data center. They're maintaining a cloud data center or partner also, right? Now, AI doesn't change any of that, right? AI just is an overlay on top of that. So, now you use AI to access the applications running in the cloud. Depending on the type of applications you're running, those applications will get infused with AI. And you have an AI overlay on top of those applications. The same thing goes for what they're doing inside their enterprises, right? The only thing is that the cloud AI overlay that is happening in the cloud is happening much faster, right? Because the hyperscalers, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Amazon, they're very AI-savvy. So, they're able to bring AI capabilities into all their cloud offerings a lot faster than an enterprise that has its own data and its own tools internally can do. So, bringing AI capabilities natively to a Fortune 500 company, for instance, will take much longer than their applications running in the cloud at, say, Microsoft Azure will become AI-friendly a lot faster, right? So, I think that's the only thing that you're seeing. It's not like they're looking to pull back stuff that was running in the cloud back into their organizations because they left the organization in the first place because they were not concerned about the data that they were accessing.

items.question: Why do you prioritize the US market as other countries build out their own compute and AI infrastructure?
items.object: Prioritizing the US market before expanding into sovereign AI markets and the global south
items.answer: I'm spending just the right amount of time, not too much. I think we are focused a lot on the US market because that is where the opportunity will emerge, and then eventually it will diffuse into other countries in the global south, right? So, I think we want to start at the source of the problem, not go to the destination directly. So, I think we're starting at the source where a lot of the innovation is happening. People are trying to figure out how to deploy these solutions, what makes the most sense, which applications really need it, which applications don't. Where does it work well, where does it not work well? Once those questions have been answered, then it will diffuse into a lot of the sovereign applications, into a lot of the enterprise applications. We'll ride that diffusion process. But it has to start from the source, you know.

items.question: How do you assess D-Matrix’s ability to secure chip supply as demand for compute and memory grows?
items.object: D-Matrix’s chip supply outlook amid growing demand for compute and memory
items.answer: Well, the chips are going to be in short supply for the next, call it 3 to 4 years at least, if not more. We have memory chip shortage. We have compute shortage, right? There's a reason why Elon wants to build his own terrafab, right? Because he feels that TSMC cannot meet all the demand for compute and memory. So, we'll see how that goes. And Intel is helping him out with that. So, we'll have to see how it all works out. But I think for the demand that we have, D-Matrix, if I would look at the D-Matrix demand picture for the next, call it, 5 years, I think TSMC's got plenty of supply to meet our demand. We are a small company. We're looking to grow into this opportunity. This opportunity is also very nascent. It's just exploded on the scene literally in the last few months. It's got a long, long way to go. So, I think we are growing into an opportunity that's pretty new. And the choices we have made on how we build our product, like we don't use the bleeding edge process technology at TSMC. We use kind of N minus 1, N minus 2 process nodes. We don't use any HBM technology. We don't use any CoWoS technology. So, all these decisions that we made early on help us. Will it be tough? Yes, for everyone. Tough for us, tough for everyone else. But I think we have a better shot at making supply because of the choices we made.

items.question: How do you think about the risk that TSMC’s supply capacity could constrain d-Matrix’s growth?
items.object: TSMC supply constraints and d-Matrix’s growth
items.answer: Not yet. Not yet. But it'll be a good problem to have, right? I mean, if I get to the point where my growth is constrained by how much TSMC can supply to me, I think I'm in a good place, right? I think then I would have to just work through the problem, which we will work through with them, right? And to me, I think it comes down to the relevance of the problem, right? If your problem that you're solving is very relevant and there's lots of big customers who care about solving the problem. Yes, you have relationships, and that's all great. But at the end of the day, follow the money, right? I think if there's a very relevant, large problem that a very relevant, large customer is trying to solve, and we think we are helping solve that type of problem, then the supply chain will make room for you, right? Because the world needs this, right? So, I think they'll find a way to make room for you.

items.question: How do you think agentic AI fits into the market for AI coding tools?
items.object: Agentic capabilities in AI coding tools
items.answer: So, agentic, I think, is not a separate—agentic is a capability that I think pretty much every company that is building a coding tool is embracing or introducing into their product offering. Right? So, I don't think you should look upon it as, okay, there is a segment of companies that's only working on agentic, because agentic is a capability that is now being—OpenClaw demonstrated what's possible. But now you take that capability and introduce it into your products, right? So, everyone is doing it. OpenAI is doing it. xAI is doing this. Obviously Anthropic, because they sell into the enterprise, they're doing it faster than anyone else. But it's a capability, right? And that capability adds more inference needs on top of the coding generation tools that already need inference, right?

items.question: How do you think d-Matrix should approach the breadth of customer demand for its technology?
items.object: d-Matrix's customer opportunity and pace of expansion
items.answer: We are working with everyone, right? I mean, we're working with all the frontier labs that build coding tools, agentic coding tools. We're working with frontier labs that are building video agents, voice agents. We're working with AI native startups building voice agents. We just have to be careful about not going too broad because I think the company is still not at the stage where we can support all these customers simultaneously. So we have to gradually grow into this opportunity with the right company. But we're doing it with everyone because it's relevant. Again, going back, what we're building is relevant for everyone. Everybody wants it. It's not like there's somebody who says, "I don't care about high levels of interactivity. I don't care that my users are able to interact with my application in real time." Nobody's telling us that, right? Everyone wants fast tokens.

items.question: How do you see the potential for AI-only companies to reshape different parts of the economy?
items.object: AI-only companies and their potential to reshape the economy
items.answer: I think it depends on what kind of product offering or products or what kind of service you're building. I mean, you have those companies today, even pre-AI, right? There were people running a consulting practice, a one-person company for a long time, and now I just use AI as an augmentation tool. So, it really depends on the product offering and service, right? I mean, there are a lot of companies that had a product offering or a service that can be taken over by AI completely, right? And you don't really need humans for the kind of work that they were doing. So, they will be the low-hanging fruit, I would say, that will immediately get consumed. Either they embrace it or then you have a new breed of companies that come and say, "Wait a minute. Why do those companies have humans in those companies? We can just do it with AI." And then they will just become a lot more efficient. Or those companies embrace it themselves and reskill the humans into something else, right? Or they find that as an opportunity for those companies to grow into something different. Because humans are good at something AI is not good at. So, why don't you reskill the humans to do stuff and expand the opportunities you can go after, as opposed to sticking with what you have? It's really an opportunity for everyone to grow into something new. But absolutely, there'll be many more companies that will be tooled only with AI to address those products and those services, right? But then there are certain products and services you really just cannot build with AI only. I mean, you need manufacturing lines and you need good product design, and there's emotion that goes into how the product is sold and how the messaging is done, and how you appeal to consumers. I mean, all this is something that you need humans for. Because at the end of the day, you're making a sale to a human. At the other end is a human who's buying the product, and you want to appeal to their sensibility and their emotions. So, not every section of the economy is going to get consumed by AI-only companies, but there will be a lot of them, a sizable portion.

items.question: What do you find most exciting about AI’s potential in healthcare?
items.object: AI's potential in healthcare and its goals for humanity
items.answer: We are not very active in the healthcare space, so I can't meaningfully comment on what's the latest and greatest is there. Because, see, we serve the tools. The tools get used by various verticals, right? Healthcare is certainly one of them. But I think to me, the most exciting thing in healthcare is really drug discovery, disease curing, really complex diseases, producing new forms of treatments that could accelerate the development of drugs or find cures, right? I think that segment is a lot more exciting. And that is one of the goals of AI—should be one of the goals of AI—is, yes, more equitable wealth distribution, sure. But really, can we make health benefits broadly available and easily accessible to parts of the population that don't even have access to it? And so, can we get humanity to a point where everybody has enough, they can live long, healthy lives, and they can live peacefully? I mean, that's maybe the third quest. We're now moving maybe into a bit of a utopian vision here, but that would be the vision, right? There's enough wealth for everyone, enough health for everyone, enough peace for everyone, and then AI has really helped humanity, right?
